Whether you are requesting a product demonstration or a quote, ordering parts, or making a service appointment, you've come to the right place. Tennant professional representatives are ready with answers to your questions, and we look forward to showing you how much we appreciate your business.

title: Top 7 Environmental Compliance Software Features | Validere
summary: The seven environmental compliance software features that matter most—why they affect operations, what to look for, and questions to ask vendors.
body_text: Most environmental teams do not lose control of compliance because they cannot run a calculation or complete a report. They lose control in the handoffs. Field inspections sit waiting for review. Permit conditions change without reaching the right people. Production data lives in one system while emissions calculations live in another. By the time reporting deadlines arrive, teams spend more time reconciling information than managing compliance. That is the problem environmental compliance software is supposed to solve. By the time most organizations begin evaluating vendors, they already know they need a platform. The harder question is which capabilities actually determine whether that platform succeeds in production. Nearly every vendor advertises inspections, dashboards, reporting, analytics, mobile applications, and document management. Those labels have become table stakes. What separates successful implementations is how those capabilities work together. The strongest environmental compliance platforms are rarely the ones with the longest feature lists. They are the ones where every capability supports the next step in the compliance process: moving work from field activity and operational data through calculations, approvals, reporting, and audit evidence without creating new bottlenecks. This guide focuses on the seven capabilities that matter most in real operations. It is not a step-by-step buying process. For requirements mapping, demo scripts, proof-of-concept testing, and scorecards, use the companion guide on how to choose environmental compliance software . For how environmental compliance fits within broader energy EHS programs, see EHS management software for energy compliance reporting . Quick answer The environmental compliance software features that matter most are automated regulatory reporting, centralized environmental data, configurable workflow automation, mobile field data capture, environmental monitoring and emissions calculations, audit-ready traceability, and enterprise governance with facility-level flexibility. Treat them as connected capabilities, not a module checklist. Two platforms can advertise the same seven features and still differ substantially in how they handle missing data, methodology changes, corrections, and multi-site governance. Judge each capability against your own workflow, then use the how-to-choose guide when you are ready to structure demos and a proof of concept. Looking for a complete buying framework? This article focuses on what capabilities matter . If you are building a shortlist, planning demonstrations, or comparing vendors, read How to Choose Environmental Compliance Software. Why capabilities matter more than feature lists Most environmental compliance software comparisons start with feature matrices: dashboards, mobile applications, inspections, reporting, analytics. Two vendors can check every box on that list and still deliver completely different operational outcomes. Consider a routine environmental inspection at a compressor station. On a feature checklist, the workflow ends when someone submits the inspection. In production, that same inspection might trigger a corrective action, notify multiple reviewers, update permit documentation, generate evidence for a future audit, and contribute data to a greenhouse gas inventory months later. Software that supports that entire chain creates value far beyond software that simply stores the form. That distinction, connected workflows versus isolated modules, is what separates platforms that help organizations scale from platforms that become another system teams have to manage. It is also the lens for the rest of this guide. Key takeaway The most valuable environmental compliance software doesn't simply digitize inspections or generate reports. It connects environmental data, workflows, approvals, calculations, and reporting into one governed process. Environmental compliance software features checklist Use this while reviewing vendor materials or sitting through a demonstration. Rather than confirming that a capability exists, ask how well it supports your operational workflows. For a full evaluation scorecard that includes implementation, security, and total cost of ownership, use the scorecard in the how-to-choose guide. Capability Why it matters Questions to ask Automated regulatory reporting Reduces manual reporting effort while adapting to changing requirements Can templates and calculations change without custom development? Centralized environmental data Creates a trusted record across facilities and systems How is data synchronized with operational systems? Configurable workflow automation Standardizes reviews, approvals, and corrective actions Can workflows differ by facility while corporate governance holds? Mobile field data capture Improves data quality by removing manual transcription Does the app support offline inspections, photos, and GPS? Monitoring and calculations Produces consistent, defensible environmental results How are methodologies maintained and versioned? Audit-ready traceability Makes every reported value explainable Can values be traced back to their original source? Enterprise governance Supports consistency across multiple facilities How are corporate standards enforced while sites keep flexibility? Environmental compliance software features checklist. Compare how vendors support each capability, not whether the label appears on a feature sheet. Figure 2. Environmental compliance software delivers the most value when monitoring, field data collection, validation, workflows, calculations, reporting, and audit evidence operate as a connected process. These seven capabilities are not independent features—they're stages in a connected compliance process. Environmental monitoring feeds field collection, field collection supports validation, validation drives approvals, approvals enable reporting, and every step contributes to the audit evidence behind the final submission. Weakness at any stage eventually appears downstream. That's why experienced buyers evaluate how a platform connects these workflows rather than whether it simply includes each feature. Environmental compliance workflow — monitoring, field collection, validation, workflow, calculations, reporting, and audit evidence Figure 3. Enterprise environmental compliance software should standardize governance, reporting, and calculation methodologies while allowing individual facilities to configure inspections, workflows, permits, and operational processes. Where to prioritize based on your biggest gap Not every organization should weight the seven capabilities equally. Start with the operational friction you already feel: If your organization struggles with… Prioritize… Manual reporting and last-minute consolidations Automated regulatory reporting Multiple facilities with inconsistent processes Enterprise governance with facility-level flexibility Spreadsheet calculations that differ by site Environmental monitoring and emissions calculations Weeks of scramble before an audit Audit-ready reporting and traceability Data scattered across SCADA, field apps, and shared drives Centralized environmental data Slow or lost approvals and corrective actions Configurable workflow automation Paper or re-keyed inspections from remote sites Mobile field data capture Use that table to focus demos. Then pressure-test how each prioritized capability connects to the next step in the workflow, not whether it appears as a module name. 1. Automated regulatory reporting Environmental reporting rarely becomes simpler over time. Every new acquisition, facility, permit, or reporting framework introduces another layer of work. The software should absorb that complexity, not your team. Spreadsheets and email approvals can hold for a single facility. Across a portfolio of compressor stations, processing plants, and terminals, the same approach becomes the reason reporting slips. The distinction that matters is not whether software can generate a report. It is whether it can run a reporting process . Imagine preparing a quarterly greenhouse gas submission for twenty compressor stations. Production data arrives from operational systems. Approved methodologies are applied. Results move through technical review and management approval. Supporting documentation stays attached to every reported value. If a regulator asks for clarification months later, the team needs to explain exactly how each number was produced, without rebuilding the story from shared drives. Strong platforms automate that workflow. Weaker ones mainly export a PDF from a dashboard. Under the U.S. EPA Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program , covered facilities follow defined reporting requirements, and Subpart W for petroleum and natural gas systems shows how much sits behind a single reported value: source categories, calculation methods, missing-data procedures, and recordkeeping. A platform that cannot absorb changes to that logic will quietly push the work back onto the team. What to look for: configurable templates and schedules; automated generation from governed data; support for multiple frameworks; approval before submission; version history; calculation logic that can change without rebuilding the program. During the demo, ask to see a complete report beginning with operational data, not a prepared dashboard export, and how templates and methodologies change without custom development. Common pitfall: Vendors often describe dashboard exports as "automated reporting." If they cannot show source data → calculation → approval → submission, they are selling a chart, not a reporting process. 2. Centralized environmental data Environmental compliance depends on information that almost never exists in one place. Production data may come from SCADA or historians. Inspection records live in mobile applications. Permit documentation sits in SharePoint or shared network drives. Laboratory results arrive through another system. Emissions calculations often still live in spreadsheets maintained by individual teams. None of those systems are broken. The problem is that none of them were designed to tell the complete environmental story, so environmental teams become responsible for stitching them together every reporting cycle. Two facilities can report the same emissions using completely different assumptions, approvals, and evidence trails. The reports may match. The evidence behind them often does not. Centralization is not about putting data in one place. It is about giving everyone confidence they are looking at the same answer. A strong platform creates a trusted environmental record by connecting the systems organizations already rely on. For most industrial operators, full replacement is neither practical nor necessary. The more important question is whether the platform can bring together the information needed for reporting, inspections, calculations, and day-to-day environmental management without forcing a parallel set of spreadsheets outside the system. That makes integration with existing operational and enterprise systems an important part of the evaluation. During the demo, ask to see a live feed from an operational system, then press on how duplicates are handled, whether historical records keep their context, and whether a user can see where an imported value came from and when it changed. Integration quality often matters more than any polished feature screen. 3. Configurable workflow automation Every environmental workflow starts with a relatively simple task. An inspection identifies a missing record. A monitoring system flags an anomaly. A permit renewal approaches its deadline. None of those activities are difficult on their own. The complexity comes from everything that happens afterward: review, corrective action, documentation, deadlines, and evidence that still has to be available years later. When those handoffs depend on email, spreadsheets, or individual memory, work falls through the cracks, and the gap usually surfaces during an audit, not during the original inspection. The common mistake is assuming standardization means uniformity. A refinery, processing facility, compressor station, and pipeline segment all have different operational realities. Corporate governance should remain consistent; execution has to reflect local permits, assets, and regulatory obligations. Platforms that force every site into one process create friction. Platforms that let every site invent its own create inconsistent reporting and weak enterprise oversight. The best workflow is often the one users barely notice, because the next step happens without a chase email. Pressure-test this by asking whether environmental teams can configure workflows without vendor support, whether approval processes can vary by facility while corporate rules stay fixed, and what happens when a corrective action becomes overdue. Then have the vendor follow one real inspection from creation through corrective action, approval, closure, and reporting. That end-to-end path reveals more than any workflow diagram on a slide. Remember A workflow isn't complete when someone submits a form. It's complete when the issue is reviewed, resolved, documented, and ready to support future reporting and audits. 4. Mobile field data capture Compliance work starts where operations actually happen: well pads, compressor stations, tank batteries, gathering systems, terminals, and refineries. If information is incomplete or inaccurate at the point of collection, every downstream step inherits the problem. Many teams still rely on paper forms or spreadsheets that someone re-enters later. That handoff creates delay, transcription errors, and missing documentation that often surfaces only when reporting or an audit begins. Digitizing a form is not the goal. Capturing information once, and making it available throughout the compliance process, is. On an LDAR route across remote facilities, inspectors document observations, attach photographs, record equipment identifiers, and flag components requiring follow-up. When connectivity returns, findings should synchronize, create work items, notify supervisors, and preserve evidence. Offline capability means creating and editing inspections without a signal, not merely viewing existing records. What to look for: full offline capture with automatic sync; photo, document, and GPS tied to the record; configurable templates by facility or permit; validation at the point of entry. One simple way to evaluate this: ask whether the app works fully offline, how it reconciles on sync, whether inspectors can capture photos, documents, and GPS during an inspection, and how quickly field data becomes available for reporting. 5. Environmental monitoring and emissions calculations Collecting environmental data is only the beginning. Organizations still need to transform that information into defensible emissions calculations, regulatory reports, and business decisions. That is where many compliance programs become vulnerable. Organizations with complex air emissions and greenhouse gas programs may also require dedicated Air & GHG management capabilities for measurement, calculations, forecasting, regulatory reporting, and audit evidence. One facility updates an emissions factor while another continues using last year's methodology. A spreadsheet formula changes without documentation. A reported value cannot be reproduced six months later because no one remembers which assumptions were applied. Those problems rarely appear while calculations are being performed. They appear during an audit, or when a corporate team tries to consolidate thirty facilities into one inventory. Most reporting errors are process failures disguised as calculation errors. Teams should always be able to answer three questions: Which source data was used? Which methodology generated this value? Can we reproduce this result exactly as it was originally reported? The EPA's AP-42 emissions factors illustrate why factor sources and calculation references have to be traceable rather than buried. Under programs such as the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program , methodology changes are expected. Software should absorb them without forcing a rebuild, and without losing the ability to reproduce a prior period as submitted. For complex emissions programs, also compare this capability against dedicated emissions management software. The best question you can ask is whether a historical report can be reproduced using the methodology that applied at the time, and how methodologies are versioned when requirements change. Follow with how validation works before reporting, how inconsistent or missing data is surfaced, and whether your team can change calculation logic without a services engagement. 6. Audit-ready reporting and complete traceability Most environmental teams do not prepare for audits once the auditor arrives. They prepare every day. Every inspection, approval, calculation, document revision, and reported value either strengthens or weakens the organization's ability to defend its compliance program months later. When evidence has to be reconstructed from spreadsheets, email chains, and shared folders, teams spend weeks answering questions they should already know the answers to. Picture a regulator asking about an emissions value submitted eight months ago. A capable platform should surface the original operational data, the methodology and factors applied, supporting field observations, who reviewed and approved the result, when changes were made, and why, in minutes rather than as a reconstruction project. The EPA's Audit Policy is a useful reminder that compliance programs depend on discovering, documenting, and correcting issues. Software should support that evidence trail; it cannot replace the judgment behind it. An audit log that shows a user changed a value is not enough. A defensible process shows where the value originated, how it was transformed, which methodology applied, what evidence supports it, and who approved it. Audit readiness is not a feature. It is the outcome of a platform that preserves evidence throughout the entire compliance process. A useful test: ask the vendor to pick a value in a sample report and walk backward through every material step, including a correction after approval. Confirm that approval history is permanently retained and that a previous reporting period can be reproduced exactly as submitted. 7. Enterprise governance with facility-level flexibility Enterprise environmental programs operate in constant tension between consistency and flexibility, and this is where buyers should spend the most scrutiny. Corporate teams need standardized reporting, common calculation methodologies, shared approval processes, and consistent governance. Individual facilities need something different. A refinery should not operate like a compressor station. A pipeline should not follow the same inspection schedule as a gas processing facility. Different permits create different obligations; different assets require different inspections; different operations introduce different environmental risks. Trying to force every facility into one standardized process creates unnecessary operational friction. Allowing every facility to invent its own creates inconsistent reporting, fragmented governance, and greater audit risk. Neither extreme scales. The strongest platforms treat governance and execution as different problems. Corporate teams establish reporting standards, methodologies, approvals, and oversight. Facilities configure inspections, workflows, permits, schedules, and operational processes that reflect local reality. Consistency without rigidity is what lets an environmental program grow without drowning sites in irrelevant process or losing enterprise control. Corporate governance versus site flexibility — corporate teams establish governance, approvals, methodologies, and reporting while facilities configure inspections, permits, assets, schedules, and workflows Figure 4: Corporate governance vs. site flexibility. Corporate standards stay fixed; facility execution adapts to local permits, assets, and conditions. In the room, ask them to show how two facilities with different permits operate inside the same environmental program, then how organization-wide reporting requirements are enforced, whether permissions can vary by business unit, and how a governance change is deployed across many sites at once. That comparison often reveals how flexible the platform really is. Common mistakes when judging environmental compliance software features Because most platforms advertise similar modules, it is easy to confuse a feature label with a working capability. These mistakes are about misreading features, not the full buying process (covered in the how-to-choose guide). Mistake Better approach Comparing feature lists Compare operational workflows Treating dashboard exports as automated reporting Ask vendors to complete a report from source data through approval Ignoring integrations behind "centralized data" Trace how operational data actually moves into the platform Assuming one workflow fits every facility Test multi-site governance with two different site types Judging only today's requirements Ask how templates, methodologies, and workflows change over time Treating compliance as document storage Follow review, approval, correction, and evidence — not just file uploads One useful exercise during demonstrations: give every vendor the same scenario. Ask them to show how an inspection moves from field collection through approvals, calculations, reporting, and audit preparation. That workflow usually reveals more than an hour of feature screens. Buying tip During demonstrations, ask vendors to complete one realistic compliance scenario from field collection through regulatory reporting instead of showing individual product features. Feature-level questions to ask every vendor Instead of asking whether software includes a feature, ask vendors to demonstrate how that feature supports your operational process. When the answer is "yes, the platform does that," ask them to show it. Capability Pressure-test question Regulatory reporting Can you demonstrate a complete report beginning with operational data? Environmental data How does information stay synchronized across systems? Workflow automation Can workflows differ between facilities while governance holds? Field operations Can inspectors complete and sync work without network connectivity? Calculations How are methodologies updated, and can historical reports be reproduced? Audit readiness Can every reported value be traced back to its source and approvals? Governance How do two different facilities operate under the same corporate standards? For a full demo brief — requirements context, exception scenarios, and a structured script — use the how-to-choose guide. Download: Environmental compliance vendor questions checklist → — a one-page version of these questions for demos. Figure 4: Capability questions checklist — bring into each demonstration, then use the how-to-choose guide for the broader evaluation process. Frequently asked questions What features should environmental compliance software include? At a minimum: automated regulatory reporting, centralized environmental data, configurable workflow automation, mobile field data capture, environmental monitoring and emissions calculations, audit-ready traceability, and enterprise governance with facility-level flexibility. The right combination depends on your regulatory environment and operating model. Judge how those capabilities connect — from field data through calculations, review, reporting, and evidence — rather than whether each appears on a feature list. How is environmental compliance software different from EHS software? Environmental compliance software focuses on environmental regulations, reporting, permits, emissions, and environmental performance. EHS software is broader: it typically includes environmental compliance alongside health and safety capabilities such as incident management, occupational safety, training, and risk management. Many platforms combine both, but organizations with complex environmental reporting often place greater weight on environmental workflows and regulatory reporting when they compare feature sets. Can environmental compliance software automate regulatory reporting? Yes — but "automated reporting" is one of the most overstated feature claims in the category. Strong platforms can collect operational data, apply calculations, route reports for approval, and generate regulatory documentation. Weaker ones mainly export a dashboard. Confirm how templates, calculations, and regulatory updates are maintained, and ask the vendor to demonstrate a complete report starting from source data. Ask the vendor to demonstrate a complete report beginning with source data, including calculations, review, approval, corrections, and final output. Does environmental compliance software support emissions reporting? Many environmental compliance platforms include emissions reporting or integrate with dedicated emissions management software . Typical capabilities include emissions calculations, greenhouse gas inventories, environmental monitoring, and supporting documentation. Confirm the platform supports your specific methodologies and reporting requirements — not only a corporate GHG total. Which environmental compliance software features matter most for multi-site industrial operators? Enterprise governance with facility-level flexibility, centralized environmental data, configurable workflow automation, and audit-ready traceability usually carry the most weight. Corporate teams need consistent methodologies and reporting standards; facilities need different permits, inspections, and local workflows. Platforms that force every site into one process — or that allow every site to invent its own — both fail at scale. Pair this judgment with the evaluation steps in the how-to-choose guide. From features to confidence Environmental compliance software is easy to compare on paper. Most platforms advertise reporting. Most promise automation. Most include inspections, dashboards, workflows, and analytics. The difference only becomes visible once real operational complexity enters the picture: different facilities, changing regulations, multiple reviewers, incomplete field data, methodology updates, unexpected audits. That is where connected workflows matter more than feature lists. The best environmental compliance software does not simply make reporting faster. It gives environmental teams confidence that the information they are using is complete, current, and defensible. That is what buyers should ultimately evaluate. Not whether a platform includes another feature. Whether it makes environmental compliance easier to operate every day. When you are ready to turn that judgment into a shortlist, demos, and a proof of concept, use how to choose environmental compliance software. For organizations managing environmental compliance across dispersed assets, regulatory programs, and operational data sources, platforms such as Validere are built to connect environmental data, calculations, workflows, and reporting across existing systems, so teams spend less time coordinating disconnected tools and more time managing the compliance program itself. title: Personalizing Airbnb search by learning from the guest journey
summary: How we built a Transformer-based sequence model that encodes years of guest behavior to surface the right listings at the right time.
body_text: By: Daochen Zha , Chun How Tan , Xin Liu , Bin Xu , Han Zhao , Xiaowei Liu , Jun Shi , Tracy Yu , Hui Gao , Huiji Gao , Liwei He , Michael Kinoti , Stephanie Moyerman , and Sanjeev Katariya Introduction Planning a trip on Airbnb rarely happens in a single session. A guest searching for a place to stay in San Francisco might browse dozens of listings over several days, leaving behind a trail of views. Typically, over a period of years, that same guest will have accumulated many previous bookings, reviews, and the occasional cancellation. Taken together, these events reveal a great deal about what that guest values in a stay. For years, Airbnb’s search ranking captured this through hand-crafted features: aggregated statistics such as total past bookings or average listing price. These worked well, but as the feature count grew into the hundreds, the approach became harder to scale and increasingly limited in expressiveness. In this blog post, we describe how we built a sequence modeling system that encodes the full guest journey using a Transformer, learning richer representations of guest preferences to deliver more personalized search results. An example of a guest journey, which is typically long, exploratory, and complex. Challenges Event sequences per guest present three core challenges. First, they are dominated by listing views, which account for the vast majority of all events — some guests accumulate hundreds of thousands of them — making raw sequences computationally intractable to model directly. The distribution of event types, with the majority being listing views. Second, unlike social media platforms, which optimize for engagement, Airbnb optimizes for booking conversion. Bookings are rare, compared to events, and deliberate, whereas a listing view could reflect genuine intent or simply idle browsing. Building a model that generalizes from these sparse, noisy signals to surface the listings most relevant to a guest is fundamentally different from social media engagement modeling. Third, training a sequence model on hundreds of millions of search-label pairs is expensive; targeted optimizations are needed to reduce costs and improve the throughput of model training. Solution Designing the guest sequence How to tackle this challenge, which is also a rare opportunity to use Transformer technology to improve guest experience? After research into similar use cases, we came up with a plan of action. Rather than modeling all events uniformly, we split the guest sequence into two parts: The long-term sequence captures infrequent but informative events from the past seven years: bookings, reviews, cancellations, and other past interactions. We cap this sequence at 80 events. The short-term sequence captures listing views from the past 21 days. We cap the short-term sequence at 200 events. The 80-event and 200-event capping thresholds are set so that only the longest 2% of sequences are truncated. Together, the two sequences give the model both depth from a guest’s booking history and the immediacy of their most recent browsing activity. Events are encoded using a shared feature pool with a unified embedding table [1] for high-cardinality IDs such as listing and host identifiers, along with hierarchical geographic IDs. An overview of our solution. Making training & serving efficient We’ve implemented three strategies that, together, deliver roughly a 4x improvement in training throughput. The most impactful is batching of searches. Consider a guest who performs three searches — at T=4, T=7, and T=10 — interspersed with events at other timestamps. Because our encoder uses a causal mask, it processes the sequence cumulatively. The embedding produced at position T=3 captures everything the guest has done up to that point, making it the correct sequence representation for the search at T=4. Similarly, no events are ignored between searches: the embedding at T=6 captures the entire sequence from T=1 through T=6 to serve the search at T=7, and the embedding at T=9 captures the full history up to T=9 to serve the search at T=10. Rather than running the encoder three separate times from scratch, we run it once over the full event sequence and route each search to its corresponding intermediate embedding, allowing three searches to share a single encoder forward pass. An illustration of batching of searches. The other two strategies reduced padding waste. (Data is processed in fixed chunks, and empty space in actual data is filled with zeros, referred to as “padding.”) To minimize padding within batches, we bucketize sequences by length. And to eliminate padded searches from the ranking model, we use sparse calculation of searches. The serving design reflects the same efficiency principle. Running a multi-layer Transformer encoder over a full guest sequence — spanning up to seven years of events and 21 days of views — at query time would be expensive. Instead, we decouple the two stages of inference. The sequence encoder runs as a daily batch job, processing event history and storing the resulting embeddings for guests who have generated new events. When a guest performs a search, the ranking model retrieves their stored embedding in real time and combines it with the live search query, then uses the information to produce scores for the retrieved listing candidates. This split keeps latency low at serving time, while still incorporating the full depth of a guest’s history into every ranking decision. An illustration of model serving. Three milestones Before rolling out any changes, we rigorously evaluate them using A/B testing, where guests are randomly but consistently assigned to either our current model or a new model. These tests typically run for three weeks, during which we closely monitor key business metrics and “guardrail” metrics to ensure there are no unintended negative side effects. A new model is only launched if there is strong, statistically proven evidence that it improves the guest experience without failing any safety checks. Following this standard, we rolled out the system in three stages. First, we tested the system with the long-term sequence alone, establishing that sequence-learned guest representations could meaningfully improve our existing ranking system. Second, we added the short-term view sequence, which introduced data scaling challenges that are addressed by the efficiency strategies above. Third, we introduced a setwise ranker [ 2 , 3 ], co-trained with the sequence encoder. Unlike a pointwise ranker that scores each listing independently, the setwise ranker considers a set of candidates together, allowing it to reason about relative differences across listings. Combined with the rich guest representations from the sequence encoder, it can make more personalized ranking decisions by jointly understanding the guest’s travel history and how the retrieved listings compare to each other. Results Offline, the long-term sequence alone improved Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG) of booking labels by +0.44% over our existing system. Adding the short-term view sequence brought the combined improvement to +1.48%. The setwise ranker added a further +2.3% improvement in offline ranking quality. In total, the improvement added up to 3.78%. At Airbnb, where the ranking model has been refined over more than a decade, a 0.3% improvement is considered significant. This substantial improvement means our model can rank the listings a guest likes higher, which may potentially help guests find what they want more easily. Online A/B tests confirmed the gains. With the long-term sequence alone: +0.31% uncanceled bookers (guests who have booked), +0.38% views. Adding the short-term sequence: +0.55% uncanceled bookers, +0.82% uncanceled nights, +0.90% views — all statistically significant. The rise in views suggests that the model is effectively surfacing listings that capture guests’ interests, which directly translates into the higher booking conversions we observed. The setwise ranker delivered a further +0.28% uncanceled bookings and +0.32% booking requesters. We also applied the system to promotional email listing ranking. Using the same sequence embeddings, without any architecture changes, produced +0.16% uncanceled bookers, +0.23% uncanceled nights, and +5.04% email clicks — demonstrating that the guest representations generalize beyond search. Conclusion What we built learns directly from the full arc of a guest’s relationship with Airbnb; their past trips, recent browsing activity, and everything in between. Moving from hand-crafted feature aggregation to learned sequence representations gives our ranking system access to a kind of guest understanding that was previously out of reach: not just what a guest has done across their history at Airbnb, but what those actions suggest about what they are looking for right now. The results across search ranking and promotional emails, which are two independently iterated surfaces, validate that this signal is both powerful and general. The work is far from finished. We are exploring near-real-time sequence embedding updates, richer event types such as wishlists and map interactions, target-aware ranking, generative recommender, and continued improvements to setwise ranking. Each of these directions builds on the same foundation: the more faithfully we can represent the guest journey, the better we can connect guests with homes they will love. For a deeper technical treatment, see our KDD ’26 paper JourneyFormer: Encoding Airbnb guest journey with sequence modeling [4]. Interested in learning more about our technical journey? Browse our previous publications to see how our systems have evolved. If tackling these kinds of challenges excites you, explore our open roles . Acknowledgments We would like to especially thank the following people for their great collaboration and for continuing to advance sequence modeling at Airbnb (listed alphabetically): Ashish Jain, Gil Forsher, Hao Li, Haozhen Ding, Jiawei Yao, Kedar Bellare, Linyun He, Mingyang Xu, Pallavi Adusumilli, Pengyu Hou, Shashank Dabriwal, Sid Reddy, Sophie Wang, Tanya Piplani, Vijay Velagapudi, Yangbo Zhu, Yan Zhang, Yi Li, Yiwei Wang, Yuli Han, and Zhiwei Wang. References [1] Coleman, Benjamin, et al. “Unified embedding: Battle-tested feature representations for web-scale ML systems.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 2023. [2] Tang, Jie, et al. “Learning to Comparison-Shop.” ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management. 2025. [3] Haldar, Malay, et al. “Beyond Pairwise Learning-To-Rank At Airbnb.” ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management. 2025. [4] Zha, Daochen, et al. “JourneyFormer: Encoding Airbnb Guest Journey with Sequence Modeling.” ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining. 2026. title: Advancing Healthcare Innovation: Segmed’s Impact at Scale
summary: Discover Segmed’s Impact Report: a nationwide, privacy-first imaging data network powering FDA-cleared AI, healthcare innovation, and equitable research.
body_text: Segmed has been advancing and conquering milestones: building a nationwide, privacy-first imaging data network spanning all 50 U.S. states, supporting more than 150 million imaging studies, and enabling over 35 FDA-cleared AI technologies. Our new Impact Report, Advancing Healthcare Innovation with Segmed , captures what this progress looks like in practice, across customers, research, healthcare providers, and the broader ecosystem. From Vision to Infrastructure Segmed was founded with a clear mission: unlock high-quality, diverse medical imaging data for research and innovation, without compromising patient privacy. Today, that vision has become infrastructure: ‍ • A network covering all 50 U.S. states • 150M+ de-identified imaging studies • Support for 35+ FDA-cleared AI solutions • Customers across 20 countries • Industry-leading certifications, including ISO27001, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA Safe Harbor , and Expert Determination This foundation enables healthcare innovators to build AI that is not only powerful, but representative, reliable, and regulatory-ready. ‍ Real-World Impact Across the Ecosystem Segmed’s impact spans the full innovation lifecycle: AI & Product Development From traditional AI validation to large-scale foundation models, Segmed datasets power training, validation, and FDA submissions across modalities including CT, MRI, X-ray, PET, pathology, and EHR-linked data. Real-World Evidence & Clinical Research Researchers leverage longitudinal, multimodal datasets to develop predictive imaging biomarkers, external control arms, and outcome-driven insights, accelerating discovery while preserving rigor. Healthcare Equity & Representation Before Segmed, deep learning models were often trained on data from just a few states. Today, AI models can be trained on patient cohorts from all U.S. states , improving generalizability and equity. Trusted by Industry and Academia Segmed partners with leading enterprises, startups, and academic institutions, supporting global research, peer-reviewed publications, and invited presentations at major conferences including RSNA, ECR, SIIM, and PMWC. Our customer feedback consistently highlights: ‍ • Speed and scale of data access • Legal and regulatory simplicity • Diversity and clinical relevance of datasets • Professionalism and trust What’s Next The Impact Report also outlines Segmed’s next chapter: ‍ • Expansion into multimodal data (EHR, pathology, molecular) • AI-driven insights layered on imaging data • Deeper engagement with pharma and life sciences • Continued investment in governance, privacy, and trust Healthcare innovation is no longer constrained by ambition: it’s constrained by access. Segmed is building the infrastructure to remove that barrier. ‍ Download and read the full Impact Report to explore the data, partnerships, and outcomes shaping the future of healthcare innovation. ‍

title: Relay.app is shutting down: How to export your workflows and move to Zapier
summary: Here's how to export your Relay.app data and rebuild those workflows in Zapier. Plus, what to expect from Zapier as a former Relay user.
body_text: Relay is shutting down on August 15, 2026, for free users, and on September 14 for paid plans. Either way, if you built workflows, agents, or tables in Relay, the end is near. The good news is that Relay has made it as easy as possible to transition your workflows to a new tool. Here's how to export your Relay.app data and rebuild those workflows in Zapier, plus what to expect from Zapier as a former Relay user. We'll also cover why Zapier is your best option compared to other Relay alternatives. Table of contents Key dates for transferring your Relay data Step 1: Export your Relay.app data Step 2: Rebuild your workflows in Zapier with Copilot Relay alternatives and why Zapier is the best fit Relay shutdown FAQ Key dates for transferring your Relay data If you have existing workflows in Relay, they'll keep running until the shutdown dates: August 15, 2026 for free users September 14, 2026 for paid accounts Every Relay user should receive an additional 25,000 steps and 10,000 AI credits to help with the transfer process. Your Relay workspace, app credentials, and tokens will be deleted automatically once your wind-down period ends. Full workspace exports can take up to 24 hours to generate, so it's best not to wait until the last minute to start the transfer process. Step 1: Export your Relay.app data Relay has made it easy for you to save your workflow information, run logs, and screenshots of your visual flows. Here's what to do to preserve your Relay.app data and get ready to rebuild in Zapier. Export your whole workspace first In your Relay.app dashboard, go to Workspace settings and click Export workspace data . This downloads a .zip file with a folder for every Workflow, Sequence, MCP Server, and Table in your workspace. Each folder includes: A build prompt (as a .md file) Run history (as a CSV) A JSON file with the workflow's exact structure A JSON file per workflow run Table data as a CSV (where relevant) Depending on how much you've built, this can take up to 24 hours to generate, and you'll get an emailed link once it's ready. That link expires in 48 hours. Grab the build prompt for each workflow you're rebuilding Relay's JSON export represents the exact structure of a workflow, but it's written in Relay's internal format, so dropping it into another tool doesn't do much on its own. If you're rebuilding in Zapier, you'll want to start with build prompts instead, which are plain-language descriptions of each workflow that are designed to be handed to an AI assistant like Zapier Copilot . Build prompts are included in your workspace .zip, but you can also grab one for a single workflow. Open the workflow, then either choose Generate prompt from the shutdown announcement widget or click the overflow menu in the top right and select Copy build prompt . Relay generates a detailed prompt describing the trigger, every step, and the logic connecting them. Click Copy prompt and paste it somewhere you can find later. Save screenshots of anything you want a visual record of Screenshots aren't part of the data export, so if you want a picture of what a workflow actually looked like, open it and choose Save workflow as screenshot . This generates images of the full workflow and each individual step, which you can download as a set or individually. Export run history if you need it for reference If you want a record of how a workflow performed historically, open its Runs tab and export the runs as a CSV. You can also open a single run and export it as JSON for details like execution history, AI chat logs, and error messages. Run data won't transfer into Zapier, but it's useful if you're troubleshooting a workflow's logic before you rebuild it, or if you just want records for your own files. Step 2: Rebuild your workflows in Zapier with Copilot Once you have your build prompts in hand, the easiest way to rebuild is with Zapier Copilot, Zapier's AI building assistant. Just describe what you want to build (or paste the workflow prompt from Relay), and Copilot proposes triggers, actions, and field mappings across Zapier's 9,000+ app integrations. 1. Open Copilot and paste your build prompt If you don't have a Zapier account, create one and log in. Then, start a new Zap—Zapier's automated workflows—from your Zapier dashboard . Paste the build prompt from Relay into the Copilot chat window. You can drop it in as-is, but it helps to add a line at the top telling Copilot what you want it to do with it, like "Rebuild this workflow using the trigger and steps described below." If the prompt is long or covers multiple distinct stages, wrap sections in headers (using markdown or XML-style tags) so Copilot doesn't blend unrelated steps together. This is more important for complex workflows with several paths or conditional branches than for a simple two-step Zap. 2. Choose "Ask as you build" for your first few migrations Copilot gives you two build modes: Auto-build , where it sets everything up and asks you to review at the end, and Ask as you build , where it checks in before making each change. For a straightforward two-step Zap, Auto-build is fine. But for anything with conditional logic, human-in-the-loop steps , or app connections you'll need to reauthorize, Ask as you build is worth the extra clicks the first time through so you can catch mismatched field mappings before they're baked in. 3. Review, connect your apps, and test Copilot will map Relay's triggers and actions to Zapier equivalents, but you'll still need to authenticate each connected app on the Zapier side and confirm field mappings look right, especially for anything Relay handled with a custom formula or a reusable Sequence. Once the Zap looks right, run a test using real data and compare the output against the run history you exported from Relay. Tweak the Zap's mapped fields as needed until the output matches your expectations. Then, publish the Zap. Relay alternatives and why Zapier is the best fit As a die-hard Zapier user even before I convinced them to hire me, I'm biased—but Zapier isn't the only place you can land after leaving Relay. n8n and Make are popular options, and either can handle your existing workflows if you're a Relay user. But I'd argue neither of them will make the transition as painless as Zapier will. n8n is built for engineering-led teams that want full control over their own infrastructure. It connects to roughly 1,500 apps, more than seven times what Relay offered, but most of that flexibility comes from writing JavaScript expressions and code nodes rather than clicking through a builder. That's the opposite of describing what you want in plain language and letting an AI assistant build it, which is what made Relay appealing in the first place. And compared to Zapier, n8n's main drawback is who owns the operational risk. Zapier handles retries, error handling, and security patches automatically, and processes 3 billion workflow runs a month without you thinking about any of it. On n8n, all of that unglamorous work—plus the hosting bill—is on you. Make is the closer cousin to Relay. Both are visual, node-based builders that reward users who are willing to learn the tool properly. Make connects to about 3,500 apps, which is more than ten times Relay's count, and its Routers, Iterators, and Aggregators give you branching logic. That power comes at a cost, though. Make's own team recommends around 19 hours of coursework before you build anything complex, and its AI cobuilder, Maia, is still in early access, so you can't yet describe a workflow in plain language the way you would in Relay or with Zapier Copilot. Zapier is the more direct upgrade for what Relay users are looking for. Relay connected to roughly 200 apps, while Zapier connects to 9,000+ apps . Zapier Copilot was also built around the same plain-language approach Relay relied on, so rebuilding a workflow should be virtually painless. And the governance you'll eventually need, like granular permissions and approval workflows backed by a full audit trail, is already built for teams at very different scales, including 69% of the Fortune 1000. Here's a detailed breakdown of how Relay and Zapier stack up for the features that matter most when you're rebuilding. Relay.app Zapier Integrations ~200 apps 9,000+ apps AI building assistant Relay AI assistant, workflow- and agent-specific Copilot, which works across Zap workflows, agentic steps, tables , and forms Conditional logic Path Path , plus step-level filters for text, number, date/time, and boolean conditions Reusable logic Sequence Sub-Zap AI agents Agent Agent (built with AI by Zapier ) Database Table Tables Custom extensions MCP Server Zapier MCP Human-in-the-loop Built-in AI output reviews Human in the loop steps Error handling Basic Autoreplay for failed steps, plus custom error handling Team permissions Basic, up to 10 users on the Team plan Granular role-based permissions , approval workflows, up to 25 users on the Team plan Security and compliance SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, OAuth-based SSO SOC 2 Type II/III, GDPR, CCPA, SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning Starting price $19/month $19.99/month AI billing AI credits (separate pool) Tasks (AI and standard actions draw from the same pool) But since you're on the Zapier blog, don't take my word for it. Slate , a digital magazine, built an agentic workflow that generated over 2,000 leads in a single month, the same kind of agent work Relay was built around in the first place. Great Day Improvements used Sub-Zap workflows, the exact feature that replaces Relay's Sequences, to automate more than 500 appointment reminders a day and lift appointment rates by 41%. Both are proof that whatever you were building in Relay, Zapier can handle it. Try Zapier free to start rebuilding your workflows before Relay's deadline hits. Try Zapier Relay shutdown FAQ How long do I have to export my Relay.app data? Free workspaces lose access on August 15, 2026. Paid workspaces lose access on September 14, 2026. Full workspace exports can take up to 24 hours to generate, and the download link is only valid for 48 hours, so it's best to start the migration process ASAP. Will my Relay workflows import automatically into Zapier? Not automatically. Relay's JSON export isn't directly compatible with Zapier's structure. The best option is to copy the build prompt Relay generates for each workflow, then have Zapier Copilot rebuild it from that description. What happens to my Relay app connections and credentials? Relay will delete all app credentials and tokens automatically at the end of the wind-down period. You'll need to reconnect each app on Zapier's side when you rebuild.
